opus-5.5.text:
I think code is almost a natural habitat for agents, for a few reasons.

First, code gives you an environment with very clear feedback. When an agent writes a piece of code, it can run it, and the compiler or the interpreter tells you immediately whether it works. Tests pass or they fail. That's very different from open-ended tasks like writing an essay, where judging quality is fuzzy. For an agent, which has to act, observe, and correct itself over many steps, having that tight, verifiable feedback loop is extremely valuable, both for doing the task and for training the model with reinforcement learning.

Second, the action space is already digital and well structured. A developer's work happens in a terminal, in an editor, in a file system, through tools like git, search, and package managers. All of these have text interfaces. So the agent doesn't need a robot arm or a complicated perception system; it can operate the same tools a human engineer uses, just through text. That lowers the barrier enormously.

Third, real software tasks are naturally long-horizon. Fixing a bug in a large repository means reading many files, forming hypotheses, trying something, seeing it break, going back. That's exactly the kind of multi-step planning and reasoning we want agents to be good at. So code is a great proving ground: if a model can handle a messy real-world codebase, it's learning skills that transfer to other agentic tasks.

And finally, there's the value side. Programming is high-value labor, and there's a huge amount of it. So the economic pull is strong, and users can feel the improvement directly. When the agent saves you an afternoon of debugging, you notice.

So for me, code sits at the intersection of verifiable, tool-rich, long-horizon, and high-value. That combination is rare, and that's why I think coding is where the agent paradigm is maturing first, and probably where we'll learn the most about how to build agents in general.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says real software tasks are naturally long-horizon and describes fixing a bug as a multi-step process.

r002.rationale: It explains that code provides a tight, verifiable feedback loop through running code and tests, and says this supports training with reinforcement learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Code is probably the most natural environment for agents, and I think there are a few reasons for that.

The first is verifiability. When a model writes code, you can run it. You get a compiler error, a failing test, a stack trace. The feedback is immediate, objective, and doesn't depend on a human sitting there judging whether the output is good. For an agent that has to take many steps and correct itself along the way, that kind of signal is everything. In most other domains, if the model makes a mistake in step three, nobody notices until the end. In code, the environment tells you right away.

The second is that the task structure already looks like what an agent does. A software engineer doesn't produce a single answer. They read the codebase, form a hypothesis, make a change, run something, look at the result, and adjust. That loop of plan, act, observe, revise is exactly the loop we want an agent to run. So we're not forcing the paradigm onto the domain. The domain was already shaped this way.

Third, the tools are already there. Terminals, version control, package managers, test frameworks, APIs. The whole ecosystem was built for one actor to operate on a system through well defined interfaces. An agent can simply plug into those interfaces. In many other fields you would first have to build the tools before the agent could do anything useful.

And then there's the reward side from a training perspective. Because the outcome is checkable, you can do reinforcement learning at scale. Did the tests pass or not? Did the program produce the right output? You can generate enormous numbers of problems with ground truth answers, and that lets the model learn long-horizon behavior rather than just imitating snippets.

Finally, code is also a kind of universal action space. If a model can write and execute code, it can indirectly do many things that aren't about software at all, like analyzing data, automating a workflow, calling a service. So improving coding ability is not just about helping programmers. It's about giving the model a general way to act in the world. That's why I think almost every serious agent effort starts from code, and why the progress there tends to show up first.

r001.rationale: It describes software engineering as a multi-step process and says code supports agents that take many steps and correct themselves, identifying its long horizon as a fit for agents.

r002.rationale: It describes a plan–act–observe–revise loop in software engineering, but does not state that code enables a closed loop in research.

astra-6.text:
I think code is especially well suited to agents because it gives you a relatively clear feedback loop. You can inspect a codebase, make a change, run it, and use the result to decide what to do next. Tests and error messages give the model concrete signals, so it can keep improving its work rather than producing an answer in one shot.

And programming naturally involves multiple steps. You need to understand the problem, find the relevant code, implement something, and verify it. Sometimes a failed test tells you that your original understanding was wrong, and you have to go back. That iterative process fits the agent paradigm very well.

Of course, passing tests doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve solved the user’s actual problem. But compared with tasks where quality is mostly subjective, code gives an agent much more direct ways to check whether it’s making progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think code is especially well suited to agents because it gives them a clear feedback loop. An agent can read the code, make a change, run it, inspect an error or a test result, and then revise its approach. It can keep moving between reasoning and action instead of having to produce a perfect answer in one attempt.

And much of the working environment is already accessible through tools: files, terminals, compilers, tests. So the agent can both do the work and check parts of its own work. Of course, passing tests doesn’t mean it has fully understood what the user wants. But that ability to get concrete feedback makes coding a particularly good setting for the agent paradigm.
